summary: Defines how LDAP distinguished names are written as text strings, using UTF-8. It tries to give a clean form for common names while being able to represent any name. It replaces RFC 1779 and was replaced by RFCs 4510 and 4514.

eli5.summary: Each entry in a directory has a full name, like a path to a file. This explains how to write that path as plain text.

subtitle: How an LDAP distinguished name is written as a readable UTF-8 string, with escaping rules and examples.

tldr.problem: X.500 directories identify entries by distinguished names encoded in ASN.1, but LDAP needs a compact text form that is easy to encode, decode and read.
tldr.mechanism: A name is written as comma-separated components in reverse order, each as type=value, with a small set of escape rules and a hex form for values with no string syntax.
tldr.outcome: It replaced RFC 1779 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 4510 and RFC 4514.

today: RFC 2253 is a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 1779. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 4510 and RFC 4514, and updated by RFC 3377.

sections.title: Background and Goals
sections.content:
The X.500 Directory uses distinguished names as the primary keys to entries. In the X.500 protocols they are encoded in ASN.1, while LDAP transfers a string representation. This specification defines that string format, which aims to give a clean representation of commonly used names while being able to represent any distinguished name.

The primary goal is ease of encoding and decoding. A secondary goal is human readability. The RFC does not expect LDAP clients with a user interface to show these strings directly to users.
sections.eli5: A directory entry has a long official name. The goal is a text version that is easy for a computer to build and take apart, and that a person can still read.

sections.title: Converting a Name to a String
sections.content:
In X.501 a distinguished name is a sequence of relative distinguished names (RDNs), each a set of one or more type and value pairs. To make the string, the RDNs are written starting with the last element of the sequence and moving backwards, separated by commas. An empty sequence becomes the empty string.

Inside one RDN, the pairs are separated by a plus sign (+) when the RDN is multi-valued, in any order. Each pair is the attribute type, an equals sign, then the value. If the type is in a published LDAP table, its short name is used; otherwise the dotted-decimal form of its OBJECT IDENTIFIER is used.

Common type strings include CN (commonName), L (localityName), ST (stateOrProvinceName), O (organizationName), OU (organizationalUnitName), C (countryName), STREET, DC (domainComponent) and UID (userid).
sections.eli5: Write the name like an address, starting from the smallest piece and ending with the biggest, with commas in between. Each piece looks like a label, an equals sign and a value, such as CN=Steve.

sections.title: Values and Escaping
sections.content:
If a value has no string form, it is written as a hash sign (#) followed by the hexadecimal bytes of its BER encoding. This form SHOULD be used when the attribute type is in dotted-decimal form. Otherwise the value is converted to UTF-8 first.

Some characters then need escaping: a space or hash sign at the start, a space at the end, and any of , + " \ < > ;. Implementations MAY escape other characters. A listed character is prefixed with a backslash; any other character is written as a backslash and two hex digits forming one byte.

Section 3 gives a BNF grammar for parsing the string back into a name, based on the grammar in RFC 822.
sections.eli5: If a name contains a comma, which is also the separator, you put a backslash in front of it so nobody mistakes it for a separator. Odd characters can be written as a backslash and two hex digits.

sections.title: Compatibility With RFC 1779 and LDAPv2
sections.content:
The syntax here is more restrictive than RFC 1779. Implementations that parse strings from an LDAPv2 client MUST accept the RFC 1779 syntax, but MUST NOT generate the RFC 1779 encodings that are not described in section 2.

Parsers MUST allow a semicolon in place of a comma, ignore spaces around separators and around =, accept an oid. or OID. prefix on numeric types, and accept a value surrounded by double quotes, inside which characters such as , = + < > the hash sign and ; need no escaping.
sections.eli5: Old programs wrote names a bit differently. New programs must understand the old way when reading, but they must only write names in the new, stricter way.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
A name with three RDNs is CN=Steve Kille,O=Isode Limited,C=GB. A multi-valued first RDN looks like OU=Sales+CN=J. Smith,O=Widget Inc.,C=US. A comma in a value is escaped as in CN=L. Eagle,O=Sue\, Grabbit and Runn,C=GB, and a carriage return is written \0D.

A value of an unrecognized type is hex: 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.0=#04024869,O=Test,C=GB. A surname with non-ASCII letters can be written in printable ASCII as SN=Lu\C4\8Di\C4\87.
sections.eli5: These samples show the rules at work: commas between pieces, a plus sign when one piece has two labels, and backslashes for tricky characters.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Distinguished names often describe real-world things, including people, and may contain a full name, an email or TCP/IP address, a physical location or organizational details. The RFC notes that most countries have privacy laws about publishing information about people.

The conversion from the X.501 form to a string is not always reversible to the same BER or DER form. For example, CN=Sam could come from either a TeletexString or a PrintableString value. Applications that need to rebuild the DER form, such as when verifying an X.509 certificate, SHOULD NOT use the string syntax and SHOULD use the hash-prefixed hex form instead.
sections.eli5: A name can reveal personal details, so be careful who sees it. Also, two different original names can turn into the same text, so for checking certificates use the exact hex form.
